The new conflict was between a rationalized theology, represented by Ashʿarism, and a form of rational thought in Arab-Islamic philosophy that was pushing strongly toward independence from its theological origins.
Al-Ghazālī became the clearest representative of one side of this new struggle: the side that historical circumstances had forced to rationalize Islamic theology.
From al-Ghazālī onward, we can see more clearly how ancient writers positioned themselves toward philosophical thought.

By this point, philosophy had become the fullest expression of the Arab-Islamic intellectual heritage. It had also entered into a dialectical interaction with major scientific achievements in physics, chemistry, astronomy, mathematics, and geography.
The effects of this interaction appeared in what we call the materialist tendencies.
Yet the dominant attitude toward philosophy among these writers came to follow the path of al-Ghazālī himself.

He turned the weapon of religious and intellectual intimidation against philosophy and the philosophers, and his approach went on to shape, to a great extent, the one-sided ways in which later Ashʿarī theologians and other historians viewed this heritage.
There are perhaps two major exceptions among the great Ashʿarī thinkers: al-Shahrastānī, the famous historian of philosophy, and Ibn Khaldūn.
Al-Shahrastānī was a model of a historian who remained faithful to historical evidence even while retaining his Ashʿarī commitments in matters of personal belief.
His theological position shaped his opinions, but not his historical investigation.
Ibn Khaldūn, as we have already said, stands out for a way of understanding history that often moves in a scientific direction. For this reason, he is much less often trapped by a one-sided view.
Hostility toward philosophy, however, began long before al-Ghazālī.
It even appeared before the time of Abū al-Ḥasan al-Ashʿarī himself.

The difference is that the earlier hostility usually came from a vague sense that philosophy posed some kind of “danger” to Islamic belief—or, more fundamentally, to the ideology of political power—without any clear understanding of what that danger actually was.
It was driven first by conservatism itself, and second by the encouragement of political rulers and those who defended their ideology.
But from the third century AH, or the ninth century CE, philosophical knowledge became an organic part of the wider intellectual world.
From that point on, hostility toward philosophy increasingly came from a more explicit awareness of the danger that new philosophical trends posed to the dominant ideology.
These were trends that took philosophical truth itself as the basis for understanding the world.
This more conscious and informed kind of opposition is what we find in the Ashʿarī current and in its greatest representative, al-Ghazālī.
By the last third of the third century AH, hostility toward philosophy was becoming increasingly severe.
Book copyists were even forced to swear that they would not copy philosophical works.
One result was that some abandoned their profession altogether.
The date of this episode places it around the rise of the Ashʿarī current.

And the fact that book copyists abandoned their trade after being forbidden to copy philosophical works tells us something else: philosophical books must have been so widely read that banning their reproduction seriously damaged the copyists’ livelihood.
Among the ancient writers, then, one-sided views of the philosophy of this period appeared in several forms.
Most of them shared a common intellectual approach dominated by supernaturalism, subjectivism, and a static, metaphysical way of thinking.

One of the first places we see this approach is in the explanations earlier writers gave for the translation movement that brought philosophical and scientific works into Arabic and became especially active under al-Maʾmūn. A famous explanation came from Ibn al-Nadīm (d. 385 AH/995 CE). He tells us that al-Maʾmūn saw Aristotle in a dream and asked him a number of questions. When al-Maʾmūn awoke, he ordered Aristotle’s books to be translated. He wrote to the Byzantine emperor asking permission to select from the ancient books of learning preserved in Byzantine lands. The emperor at first refused, but eventually agreed. Al-Maʾmūn then sent a group that included al-Ḥajjāj ibn Maṭar, Ibn al-Biṭrīq, Salm, the head of the House of Wisdom, and others. They selected the books they wanted from those they found and brought them back. Al-Maʾmūn then ordered them to translate the books, and they did.

So this is how a historical movement of enormous importance to the development of Arab-Islamic thought was explained: through a supernatural and purely personal way of thinking, and with remarkable simplicity and naivety.

What is more surprising is that later Arab-Islamic historians repeated Ibn al-Nadīm’s explanation without questioning it, almost as though it were self-evidently true. It therefore stopped being the explanation of one individual and became part of a wider way of understanding major historical events.

This way of thinking prevented those historians from seeing an important fact. The connection between Arab-Islamic thought and the ancient sciences—that is, philosophy together with logic, natural science, mathematics, and medicine—had begun before the time of al-Maʾmūn. It did not have to wait for the caliph to have his “historic” dream.

It did not have to wait because the course of history itself had already created the social pressures, intellectual exchanges, and cultural needs that gradually established this connection during the first two Islamic centuries. Aristotle could hardly have had the “honour” of appearing in al-Maʾmūn’s dream if he had not already been present in the intellectual world of the Abbasid caliphs who came before al-Maʾmūn.

And Aristotle would receive far greater attention than anything suggested by this dream, especially from al-Maʾmūn himself. Al-Maʾmūn really did play a major role in developing the connection with ancient learning. But he did so in response to the real conditions of his society and his time, not because of an accidental dream, a passing coincidence, or his own personal will.
We see the same general approach in another form when writers discuss whether the “Arab mind” was naturally capable of philosophical knowledge. Here a racial way of thinking begins to appear.
The judge Ṣāʿid al-Andalusī (d. 463 AH/1070 CE) used this kind of reasoning when he discussed the sciences among the Arabs. He wrote:

“As for philosophy, God Almighty granted them no share of it, nor did He shape their natural disposition to take an interest in it. I know of no one of Arab stock who became famous for it except Abū Yūsuf Yaʿqūb ibn Isḥāq al-Kindī and Abū Muḥammad al-Ḥasan al-Hamdānī.”

It is clear that Ṣāʿid’s generalization was not limited to pre-Islamic Arabia, even though the surrounding discussion in his book might initially suggest that it was. His judgment reaches all the way to the periods of al-Kindī and al-Hamdānī. In other words, he treats it as a judgment about Arabs as a human race in every age of their history, rather than about a particular society living under particular conditions at a particular stage of history.
We will see this racial way of thinking appear again in discussions of Arab-Islamic philosophy, both among earlier writers other than Ṣāʿid and among modern Arab researchers and Orientalists.
For the author of Ṭabaqāt al-Umam, then, Arabs were a “race” that was not naturally or instinctively suited to receiving philosophy, or to acquiring this kind of higher knowledge.
His exceptions—al-Kindī and al-Hamdānī—only serve to confirm the rule he believed he had found.

At the same time, however, Ṣāʿid did not divide the philosophers of this intellectual heritage according to their original ethnic ancestry. We can see this first from the distinction just discussed, and second from the praise and admiration he gives al-Fārābī elsewhere in the book, even though he regarded al-Fārābī as being of non-Arab origin.

Dividing the philosophers of this heritage according to their different ethnic origins does more than introduce a racial view that cannot be accepted scientifically. It also breaks apart the unity of the Arab-Islamic intellectual heritage.
That heritage cannot be broken up along racial lines.
Its unity rests on two foundations that are historically and objectively bound together: its Arab character and its Islamic character.

The heritage is Arab as a whole, whatever the ethnic origins of the people who produced it. It is Arab not simply because Arabic was its language. Its linguistic structure was also bound up with its intellectual, social, and political structure. At the same time, it was connected with philological, anthropological, and psychological structures.
Its Islamic character was equally bound up with this whole formation, in both its existence and its development. The Islamic character of the heritage cannot be separated from its Arab character.

For all these reasons, it is wrong to look at the people who created this heritage and say that one was Arab while another was not. In cultural and intellectual terms, they all belonged to the Arab tradition, and they all belonged to the Islamic intellectual world as well.
This broad category also includes non-Muslims who helped create the heritage in any of the ways known to history—for example, by translating Greek, Persian, and Indian cultures and philosophies.
Al-Shahrastānī himself fell into another kind of unrealistic and unscientific way of looking at this heritage.
Speaking of the “later philosophers of Islam,” he writes that:

“They all followed the method of Aristotle in everything he taught and in the views peculiar to him, except for a few points where they may have preferred the opinion of Plato or the earlier philosophers. Since Ibn Sīnā’s method is regarded by the group as more precise, and his investigation of realities as more penetrating, I chose to present his method from his books (...) and passed over the methods of the others. The whole prize of the hunt is there.”

To be fair to al-Shahrastānī as a scholar, we should not begin simply by criticizing the weakness in his approach that appears in this passage. Before explaining that criticism, we must recognize the major contribution al-Shahrastānī made to the history of philosophy.

His book al-Milal wa-l-Niḥal (Religions and Sects) marked something close to a whole new stage in the development of the history of philosophy as a field of study. He set out to write a history of world philosophy as it was known up to his own time.

He also seems to have had a good knowledge of the sources he used. He presented the philosophies of the Greeks, Persians, Indians, and Arabs in a connected sequence while preserving the distinctive features of each.
The work was especially important because al-Shahrastānī tried to draw a line between religion and philosophy.

This probably did not come only from something distinctive in his own education. More importantly, it came from the principle he adopted in his method of research. At that stage of history, this principle was itself highly progressive.
At the beginning of the second part of his book, he writes:

“Chapter One: the followers of opinions and sects among the Sabians, the philosophers, the views of the Arabs in the Age of Ignorance, and the views of the Indians. These stand in direct opposition to the followers of religions, as we have said. They rely on sound natural disposition, complete reason, and a clear mind.”

In this passage, al-Shahrastānī does more than distinguish religion from philosophy. He also states, quite objectively, that philosophers rely on “sound natural disposition, complete reason, and a clear mind.”

This does not contradict the dismissive language he later uses about philosophers whom he classifies as eternalists, naturalists, and metaphysicians. He was still approaching philosophy as a Muslim committed to the Ashʿarite school.
But it is important enough that he separated religion from philosophy and acknowledged that philosophy rests on principles he could not simply deny.

Al-Shahrastānī made another important contribution as well. He tried to distinguish philosophies from one another according to broad intellectual currents, rather than merely according to the personal opinions and ideas of individual thinkers.
This was one of his greatest contributions to the development of the history of philosophy.
A — Materialists or naturalists. He said that they relied on the world known through the senses, and he called them naturalist eternalists.

B — Metaphysical philosophers. He said that they accepted sensory reality and also affirmed what can be known by reason, but rejected religious laws, revealed law, and Islam. According to him, they regarded religious laws as arrangements made for the general welfare of society. Legal limits and rulings, and the categories of permitted and forbidden, were human conventions. The founders of religions, in their view, were men of practical wisdom.
In another classification, which he called his comprehensive scheme, al-Shahrastānī wrote:

“Among people are those who accept neither what is known through the senses nor what is known through reason. These are the Sophists. Some accept what is known through the senses but not what is known through reason. These are the naturalists. Some accept both the sensory and the rational but do not accept legal limits and rulings. These are the eternalist philosophers. Some accept the sensory, the rational, and legal limits and rulings, but do not accept revealed law and Islam. These are the Sabians. Some accept all of these, together with a revealed law and a form of Islam, but do not accept the revealed law of our Prophet Muḥammad. These are the Magians, Jews, and Christians. And some accept all of these. These are the Muslims.”
In this attempt by al-Shahrastānī, we can also see an early step toward distinguishing materialist philosophers from idealist philosophers.
There is another important distinction in al-Milal wa-l-Niḥal. Al-Shahrastānī sees philosophy as an arena of conflict between these two groups: the materialists and the idealists.

This was another very important principle to appear at that stage in the writing of the history of philosophy. It meant that this historian was trying to identify the source and driving force behind the development of philosophy itself.

All these principles give al-Shahrastānī’s history of philosophy great importance. Its value lies not only in the material it contains, but also in the fact that it established important principles of research that later philosophers developed further in their own works.
Yet all these major strengths do not prevent us from finding a weakness in al-Shahrastānī’s approach when he discusses the philosophers of the Arab-Islamic heritage.

His claim that they all followed Aristotle in everything Aristotle taught and in everything distinctive to his philosophy, apart from a few points where they may have preferred Plato or other earlier philosophers, is contrary both to the historical evidence and to any scientific understanding of how different cultures and philosophies interact.

As for the evidence itself, a close study of these philosophers reveals many ways in which they departed from Aristotle, even though they never made a complete break with the Aristotelian tradition. It also shows that their creative differences from Aristotle affected the foundations of their theories in important ways, especially in relation to the theory of emanation.
In the present book, we will repeatedly try to show where the philosophers of our heritage differed from Aristotle and from other earlier philosophers.

Even if we accepted the view that the work of these philosophers was limited to commenting on and interpreting classical texts, a closer look at those commentaries and interpretations would still reveal their distinctive value.

Commentary and interpretation could become independent acts of creative thought. At times they produced genuinely new ideas, from which the first seeds of new theories emerged and the foundations of an independent philosophy began to take shape.

As for the interaction between different cultures, we have already pointed out earlier in this introduction that an outside culture can influence another culture only through the internal factors already operating within the receiving society. In other words, the influence passes through the particular conditions in which that culture exists.

Those conditions may be economic, social, political, or intellectual. Underlying them is the particular kind of relations of production that exists in that society and the historical form those relations take.
This is a general objective law.

It therefore makes no sense to suppose that Arab-Islamic philosophers living in the Middle Ages, in a society dominated by its own particular form of feudal relations of production, would think in exactly the same way as Aristotle, whose philosophy reflected the conditions of the ancient world and its particular slaveholding society.
Of course, we have no right to expect al-Shahrastānī, living when he did, to have known this law, much less to have applied it.

But given the remarkable qualities he showed as a historian of philosophy, we can reasonably expect him to have noticed what the philosophers of the Arab-Islamic tradition developed independently of Aristotle and the other “earlier philosophers.”
We can also expect him to have seen, for example, what distinguished al-Kindī and al-Fārābī from Ibn Sīnā.

He should not simply have presented Ibn Sīnā’s method and ignored “the methods of the others” on the grounds that “the whole prize of the hunt is there.” That proverb proves neither a philosophical point nor even a historical one.

We have spent time on this criticism of al-Shahrastānī because his approach reflects a widespread way in which earlier writers dealt with the Arab-Islamic philosophical heritage. We find many examples of it among them, just as we also find it frequently in the work of modern Orientalists and Arab researchers.
There is another model of how earlier writers understood—or perhaps misunderstood—the heritage.

A traditionalist current arose that wanted to cut even the thin thread the Ashʿarite school had left as a formal connection between the rational method of logic and philosophy on the one hand and the traditionalist method on the other.
Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ (d. 643 AH) was at first the most extreme of the later jurists who represented this current.
He became famous for a legal ruling in which he declared the study of logic and philosophy forbidden.
